earlier_scan.source_named: Only Kieffer 1983 and Rao 1981/1995 ethnographic notes cited; no grammar or phonology of Inku located

sources.citation: Wikipedia, "Inku language" and "Peripatetic groups of Afghanistan" (wikitext, accessed 2026-09-17).
sources.note: Nothing on stress or phonology; secondary. Cites Rao 1986:266-67 (origin in Dera Ismail Khan / Dera Ghazi Khan; possible relation to Saraiki) and Rao 1995:82, 85.

sources.citation: Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig (eds.). 2019. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 22nd ed., entry "Inku" [jat]. Dallas: SIL International.
sources.note: Nothing. "No known L1 speakers. Last speakers probably survived into the 1990s.. Dialects: None known. Related to Western Punjabi [pnb]. A member of macrolanguage Lahnda [lah]." Internet Archive copy 2019-10-14 (live ethnologue.com could not be reached by automated download).

sources.citation: Hanifi, M. Jamil. 2012. "Jāt." Encyclopaedia Iranica (online edition).
sources.note: Nothing; ethnographic article. Says the Jats speak the Persian or Pashto of their hosts and claim secret languages; does not describe Inku at all. Bibliography lists Rao 1979, 1981, 1982, 1986, 1995, 2004 and Olesen 1982-2000 (all ethnographic).

sources.citation: Pstrusińska, Jadwiga. 2004. O tajnych językach Afganistanu i ich użytkownikach [On the secret languages of Afghanistan and their speakers]. Kraków: Księgarnia Akademicka. 172 pp. ISBN 83-7188-757-4. (Open access in the Jagiellonian University Repository, RUJ item 261535; Polish original of Pstrusińska 2013, Secret Languages of Afghanistan and Their Speakers, Cambridge Scholars.)
sources.note: Nothing on Inku phonology, stress or tone. Inku content is limited to: p. 116 'Używali także swych języków etnicznych, które są nieznane na prawie całym terenie Afganistanu, np. inku lub baluczi, przez co również mogli uchodzić za osobników mówiących tajemnym językiem' (they also used their ethnic languages, unknown almost everywhere in Afghanistan, e.g. Inku or Baluchi, so they too could pass for speakers of a secret language; Rao 1986:254-255); p. 117 list of self-designations from Rao 1986 (Baluć, Gorbat, Śadibaz, Vangawala, Galali, Pikrag); p. ~140 'języka urdu lub inku (lahnda) przez gru…

sources.citation: Windfuhr, Gernot L. 2002 (updated 2012). GYPSY ii. Gypsy Dialects. Encyclopaedia Iranica XI/4: 415-421 (online edition).
sources.note: names the groups and affiliation only; nothing on stress or accent

sources.citation: Rao, Aparna. 1995. "Marginality and Language Use: The Example of Peripatetics in Afghanistan." Journal of the Gypsy Lore Society, 5th series 5(2): 69-95.
sources.note: The only publication with first-hand Inku data (a Vangawala text, pp. 85ff., and remarks on the four varieties, p. 82). Needs to be read to confirm whether it has any phonological or stress remark; second-hand (Wikipedia citing p. 82) says the materials are unpublished and unanalysed, so a stress statement is unlikely but this is the one place it could be.

sources.citation: Rao, Aparna. 1994. Peripatetics of Afghanistan, Iran, and Turkey. In John Middleton & Amal Rassam (eds.), Encyclopedia of World Cultures, vol. IX: Africa and the Middle East, 274-276. Boston: G. K. Hall. (Glottolog ref 326078; read in the encyclopedia.com reprint.)
sources.note: 'within each group, a separate dialect or language is spoken. The latter are either of Indic or Iranian origin, and many are structured somewhat like an argot or secret language' - nothing on stress

sources.citation: Rao, Aparna. 1992. "Jat." In Paul Hockings (ed.), Encyclopedia of World Cultures, Vol. 3: South Asia, 110-113. Boston: G.K. Hall. (Read in the encyclopedia.com transcription.)
sources.note: Nothing on phonology, stress or tone; the linguistic paragraph is generic and concerns scripts (Urdu/Gurmukhi/Devanagari) used by South Asian Jats.

sources.citation: Kieffer, Charles M. 1983. "Afghanistan v. Languages." Encyclopaedia Iranica I/5, pp. 501-516 (online edition, iranicaonline.org).
sources.note: Nothing about Inku stress. Sections 19-22: "other Indian minority groups speak Sindhī (20) and Inku (Lahndā, 22).. Dialects of the Sirāikī (Sindkhī) type, about which relatively little is known, are used by the Vaṛŋgāwālā, the Pikrāǰ, the Šādībāz, and the Jalālī"; section 32: Rao's Jat materials "will be published in collaboration with Ch. M. Kieffer" (no such publication located). The article's only stress remark concerns Dari, not Inku. downloaded from the Internet Archive copy (2023-11-17) because iranicaonline.org could not be reached by automated download.
Nothing. Only two references (Kieffer 1983, Rao 1995), both typed overview; zero descriptive references. Note says Ethnologue's Jakati [jat] entry (29,300 speakers in Ukraine) is erroneous.

sources.citation: Rao, Aparna. 1986. "Peripatetic Minorities in Afghanistan: Image and Identity." In Erwin Orywal (ed.), Die ethnischen Gruppen Afghanistans: Fallstudien zu Gruppenidentität und Intergruppenbeziehungen, 254-283. Wiesbaden: L. Reichert. ISBN 3-88226-360-1.

sources.note: Earliest report on the Jat groups and their languages (Kieffer 1983 cites p. 144 for vocabulary of Magadi/Mogatibey); may contain a few remarks on the Indo-Aryan varieties. Ethnographic focus; low chance of a stress statement.

sources.citation: Rao, Aparna (with Ch. M. Kieffer, announced). Unpublished field materials on the languages of the Jat (Vangawala, Pikraj, Shadibaz, Jalali) collected in Afghanistan in the 1970s; announced in Kieffer 1983, Encyclopaedia Iranica "Afghanistan v. Languages", section 32 as "will be published in collaboration with Ch. M. Kieffer".

sources.note: The only primary linguistic corpus of Inku known to exist; never published as far as any bibliography shows (Rao died 2005). If it survives in an archive it is the only possible basis for a phonological statement.
